intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From sovereign heroic self-assertion to humble interdependence
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A self-asserting, dominance-oriented fantasist who renames himself, invents Dulcinea, recruits Sancho through promises, imposes chivalric categories on reality, and treats other people chiefly as audience, instruments, or obstacles to his solitary heroic mission.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: A defeated, sane man who relinquishes heroic self-assertion, confesses his madness, apologizes to Sancho, rewards household servants, submits to God and the sacraments, and dies as Alonso Quixano among family, friends, and dependents, recognizing dependence and moral debt.

trajectory.position_description: Strongly agency-driven: he manufactures a knightly identity, names horse, self, and lady, reads the inn as a castle, demands dubbing, and enlists Sancho as an instrument and audience for his romance script.
key_moments: Loses his wits reading chivalry books and decides to become a knight-errant.
Names himself Don Quixote, his horse Rocinante, and invents Dulcinea as Lady of Thoughts.
Demands to be dubbed a knight and attacks carriers who disturb his armor.
Recruits Sancho with promises of an island governorship.

trajectory.position_description: Agency remains dominant but becomes hierarchical and coercive: he commands Sancho, punishes mockery, and explains every contradiction as enchantment. Dependence on Sancho grows, but communion remains patronizing rather than reciprocal.
key_moments: Charges windmills and converts failure into the Sage Freston's malice.
Frees galley slaves and demands their embassy to Dulcinea.
Performs the Sierra Morena penance and sends Sancho to Dulcinea.
Beats or threatens Sancho over Dulcinea and the lashes.
Is caged and carted home while interpreting captivity as enchantment.

trajectory.phase: Inflated public agency and staged performance
trajectory.position_description: His agency becomes theatrical and literary: he seeks fame, printed history, staged combats, and courtly recognition. He remains commanding, but increasingly depends on Sancho, hosts, and enchanters to sustain his role.
key_moments: Undertakes the third sally and defends chivalric truth.
Experiences El Toboso disillusion and the peasant-girl enchantment.
Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and confronts the lion.
Participates in Clavileño and the staged duenna adventures.

trajectory.position_description: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon strips him of active mastery. He accepts retirement, delegates judgment to Sancho, stops Sancho's whipping out of compassion, and returns home subdued and dependent.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and must retire for a year.
Endures pig stampede, mock resurrection, and ducal humiliations.
Stops Sancho's self-flagellation when Sancho cries out in pain.
Admits his wits are confused and lets Sancho judge the peasants' dispute.

trajectory.position_description: He surrenders agency to Christian humility and communal obligation. He renounces knight-errantry, asks forgiveness, makes bequests, blesses Sancho, and dies lucid among others.
key_moments: Wakes sane and renounces books of chivalry as dark ignorance.
Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into mad knight-errantry and cancels his debts.
Calls his niece and housekeeper his daughters and provides for them in his will.
Dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The arc begins with a solitary hidalgo imposing a self-authored heroic identity on the world and commanding others as romance figures; it ends with a defeated, sane man acknowledging dependence on Sancho and his household, seeking forgiveness, and dying within ordinary Christian community.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: The axis is a recognizable critical construction: Cervantine scholarship has long described Don Quixote's trajectory from self-invented heroic identity and imposed chivalric fantasy to disillusioned sanity, confession, and Christian humility. The specific vocabulary of 'agency–communion' is modern, but the underlying intrapersonal change is supported by psychological and psychoanalytic readings of the character.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-sealing enchantment logic to lucid disenchantment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Absolute conviction that chivalric romances are literal truth and that he is a knight-errant; inns are castles, windmills are giants, strangers are knights or enchanters, and every contradiction is the work of hostile enchanters rather than his own error.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Full lucidity: he admits his madness, calls chivalry books detestable absurdities, rejects the pastoral fantasy, renounces Don Quixote, confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies sane as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Reality is wholly assimilated to romance. His identity is unquestioned, and defeats are rationalized rather than doubted.
key_moments: Dubbing at the inn and armor-watching.
Mistakes windmills for giants and blames the sage Freston.
Frees galley slaves and interprets their ingratitude as villainy.
Treats the basin as Mambrino's helmet and rationalizes its appearance.

trajectory.position_description: He can say that he pictures Dulcinea as he wishes and chooses Amadis-style penance deliberately, yet this insight is absorbed into the chivalric frame. Contradictions become proof of hostile enchantment.
key_moments: Admits poets invent ladies and that he imagines Dulcinea.
Chooses Amadis-style penance as a deliberate performance.
Describes the cave of Montesinos vision and insists on its truth.
Sees a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea and blames enchanters.

trajectory.position_description: Staged courtly adventures validate him outwardly, but the false Second Part, the Knight of the Mirrors, and doubts about the cave vision increasingly destabilize his confidence.
key_moments: Defeats the Knight of the Mirrors and explains Samson's face as an enchanter's transformation.
Hears the enchanted head and staged Merlin confirm Dulcinea's disenchantment.
Begins to doubt whether his cave vision was true.
Accepts Clavileño and Merlin literally despite earlier doubts.

trajectory.position_description: After the White Moon defeat he becomes more rational about ordinary matters such as inns and false histories, but still believes in enchantment, Sancho's penance, and omens. Delusion persists alongside genuine self-reproach.
key_moments: Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and accepts a year's retirement.
Recognizes an inn as an inn and admits his wits are confused.
Reads the hare as an omen despite earlier condemning superstition.
Still hopes for Dulcinea's disenchantment.

trajectory.position_description: The delusion breaks completely. He recognizes his madness, repents, renounces knight-errantry, and frames his former heroism as dangerous illusion.
key_moments: Wakes from fever with his reason clear and calls chivalry books detestable absurdities.
Rejects the pastoral plan as nonsense and insists he is no longer Don Quixote.
Confesses, makes a Christian will, and dies calmly as Alonso Quixano the Good.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The novel tracks a long, non-linear consolidation of delusional certitude through repeated enchantment rationalizations, followed by late doubts under staged and real mirrors, then a final deathbed recovery of reason.

historical_cultural.reasoning: The trajectory from self-sealing enchantment logic to final lucidity (the deathbed recantation, the will, the repudiation of the books) is one of the most heavily discussed problems in Cervantine criticism, and it is central rather than incidental: critics have read it psychologically (Johnson, El Saffar), philosophically as a desengaño structure (Maravall, Durán, Bandera), and historically as an erasmian 'cura' or ironic authorial imposition (Close, Riley). intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: A modest hidalgo refashions himself as Don Quixote de la Mancha, accumulates chivalric titles, treats identity as a literary script to be proved by fame, and pursues eternal renown, honor, imperial rank, and public recognition through deeds dedicated to Dulcinea and posterity.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He rejects the Don Quixote identity as madness, insists he is Alonso Quixano, renounces chivalric glory, seeks confession, charity, fidelity, and forgiveness above fame, makes a sane Christian will, and dies as Alonso Quixano the Good.

trajectory.position_description: Identity is invented through names and props: Don Quixote, Rocinante, Dulcinea, and the mock dubbing all confirm a new self. Renown is already the explicit goal.
key_moments: Takes the name Don Quixote de La Mancha after naming his horse and lady.
Believes the innkeeper's mock ceremony makes him a genuine knight.
Desires to become Emperor of Trebizond and win eternal name.
Demands the Toledo traders confess Dulcinea's beauty.

trajectory.position_description: Identity becomes increasingly public and literary: he adopts titles, treats printed history as proof of his reality, and makes honor legalistic and theatrical.
key_moments: Adopts the nickname Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
Renames himself Knight of the Lions after confronting the lion.
Defends fictional Queen Madasima with his life.
Rejoices that a printed history of his deeds exists and worries about reputation.

trajectory.position_description: His authentic identity is challenged by public performance, the false Second Part, and then shattered by the White Moon defeat. He begins to imagine a diminished pastoral alias, Quixotize.
key_moments: Seeks public vindication at Saragossa, in Barcelona, and before the duke and duchess.
Reads the false Second Part and resolves to disprove it by going to Barcelona.
Is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and calls himself the most unfortunate knight.
Plans a pastoral retirement with the alias Quixotize.

trajectory.position_description: He rejects the pastoral alias and the entire knightly self. His final identity is the sane, penitent Alonso Quixano, and salvation replaces renown.
key_moments: Calls the pastoral plan nonsense and says he is no longer Don Quixote.
Insists he is Alonso Quixano, enemy of Amadis and all knight-errantry.
Makes a will and provides for his household.
Dies as Alonso Quixano the Good, with the curate testifying to his sanity.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The identity and honor arc moves from self-naming and title accumulation through public fame and counterfeit doubles to a final deathbed rejection of the invented knight in favor of the ordinary mortal name and Christian humility.

trajectory.position_description: He acts from romance scripts, rescues Andres, frees galley slaves, and attacks supposed villains, while rationalizing harmful outcomes as ingratitude or enchantment.

Frees the galley slaves and is beaten by them.
Blames Sancho for warning him about the galley slaves and for contradicting his fantasies.

trajectory.position_description: His devotion to Dulcinea and his honor justifies coercing Sancho and dismissing Sancho's judgment, though protectiveness and gratitude occasionally break through.

Beats Sancho for disparaging Dulcinea.
Rescues Sancho during the boar hunt and defends him from the servants' prank.

Admits he is unfit to judge and lets Sancho settle the peasants' wager.
Praises Sancho as a great philosopher and accepts his counsel.

trajectory.position_description: He accepts responsibility for Sancho and his household, renounces the harmful books, apologizes, and seeks Christian forgiveness.
key_moments: Asks Sancho's forgiveness for drawing him into knight-errantry.
Cancels Sancho's debts and promises him rewards in his will.
Protects his niece from chivalry books and asks forgiveness of the false author.

trajectory.position_description: Mood swings rapidly from joy to anxiety to rage to self-pity. Violence and rhetoric are immediate responses to contradiction.

Dulcinea enchantment despair.
Castle humiliations.

trajectory.position_description: After defeat his volatility cools into melancholy, self-reproach, and resignation. He still has flashes of irritation, but the dominant tone is weary acceptance.

Calls his wits confused.
Endures pig stampede and abduction.
Returns home subdued.

trajectory.position_description: Emotional life is integrated and quiet. He is repentant, grateful, affectionate, and ready for death.
key_moments: Wakes lucid after fever.
Confesses and makes his will.

Dies calmly.

Watches the road for Dulcinea after Sancho completes the lashes.

trajectory.position_description: With the collapse of his chivalric identity, the enchantment project and pastoral fantasy around Dulcinea are discarded as part of his former illusion.
key_moments: Renounces books of chivalry.
Abandons knight-errantry and its Dulcinea project.
Dies as Alonso Quixano rather than as Dulcinea's knight.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea exists as an invoked name in prefatory verse and then as Quixote's fabrication laid over Aldonza Lorenzo. She initiates nothing and reciprocates nothing; her 'agency' is grammatical only.

trajectory.position_description: She acquires a grave, a counterfeit peasant body, and finally a speaking role in the ducal masque. Yet every apparent act is authored by others: the epitaph by academicians, the peasant body by Sancho, the voice and tears by the duke and duchess.

Chapter 88: she speaks in Merlin's masque, demanding Sancho's lashes.
Chapter 89: the masque is revealed as a ducal drollery; Merlin is a majordomo.

trajectory.position_description: She is almost wholly offstage: a postponed whipping, a curse, a pastoral name, an unpaid score. The fraudulent 'disenchantment' is announced without her presence, and Quixote's recovery of reason dissolves the world that housed her. She neither acts nor is granted a final word.
key_moments: Chapter 93: her disenchantment is scheduled for 'leisure hours.'
Chapter 103: Sancho is said to have forgotten the disenchantment entirely.
Chapter 110: Altisidora curses her to remain enchanted forever.
Chapter 113: attempted coerced flogging; sworn promise of voluntary penance; disenchantment deferred again.
Chapter 125: Sancho's lashes are counted against trees; her cure is declared accomplished by fraud.
Chapter 126: she becomes a pastoral pretext rather than a woman to be found.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea has no interiority in the text. On the agency–communion axis she never becomes an agent and never enters reciprocal communion; she is only the object of others' projections, errands, forgeries, and staged performances. The apparent 'voice' in Chapter 88 is counterfeit, so the arc remains flat.

structuralist.reasoning: The axis explicitly denies Dulcinea any interiority or independent agency, so it cannot function as an intrapersonal psychological change; it is instead a narratological claim about objecthood, projection, and ventriloquism. Scholarship on Dulcinea generally treats her as an absent ideal, a name, or a structural function in Quixote's imagination, not as a character whose beliefs, self-perception, or moral reasoning develop. I cannot recall a real published work that supports this as an intrapersonal axis for Dulcinea.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From Unwitting Construct to Unwitting Construct: self-knowledge never develops
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Dulcinea begins with no interiority, no beliefs of her own, and no awareness that she has been named, invented, or loved by hearsay.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: She ends exactly as unaware: she never learns that she is a fiction, never learns of Sancho's fraud, never learns that the disenchantment was staged, and never learns that Quixote's recovery of reason dissolves her. The text closes without granting her a single moment of self-recognition.

trajectory.position_description: She is a name and a fabricated beloved. The narrative never enters her, so self-awareness is not merely absent but structurally impossible.
key_moments: Chapter 2: Aldonza Lorenzo 'never knew it nor gave a thought to the matter.'
Chapter 10: her first concrete attribute is a marginal joke about salting pigs.
Chapter 14: Quixote admits he 'cannot say positively' whether she is pleased.
Chapter 26: she is identified as Aldonza Lorenzo, illiterate and unaware of Quixote's gaze.

trajectory.position_description: Facts accumulate around her—illiteracy, a letter she cannot read, forged commands, an epitaph—but none reaches her consciousness. Knowledge about her grows; her knowledge of herself does not.
key_moments: Chapter 27: Quixote appends 'del Toboso' and later admits the verse would be unintelligible without it.
Chapter 28: the curate supplies her with a forged command and confirms she cannot read.
Chapter 38: she survives only as the phrase 'his lady's scorn.'
Chapter 47: she is given a prophetic womb and future without being consulted.

trajectory.position_description: She receives a body, an epitaph, a counterfeit peasant double, and a speaking masque role, but she never knows that these are performances. Her apparent feelings are authored by others.
key_moments: Chapter 53: strangers bury her in verse and epitaph without her consent.
Chapter 63: a peasant girl is enthroned as her and speaks only to refuse.
Chapter 76: she flees from being addressed in the cave.
Chapter 88: she voices scripted grief and demands lashes from Sancho.
Chapter 89: the reader learns Merlin is the duke's majordomo; she never does.

trajectory.position_description: Her disenchantment is postponed, forgotten, fraudulently completed, and finally voided by Quixote's sanity. She never appears to learn any of it. The book ends without giving her a final scene or a moment of insight.
key_moments: Chapter 103: Sancho has 'forgotten all about' the disenchantment.
Chapter 110: Altisidora wishes her permanently enchanted.
Chapter 125: her cure is certified by lashes laid on trees.
Chapter 126: an omen says she will never be seen; the pastoral scheme replaces rescue with verse.
Chapter 127: Quixote dies sane and does not mention her in his will or final confession.

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Across the summaries Dulcinea is repeatedly described as having no interiority, no beliefs, no desires, and no self-awareness. Even when she is given scripted speech and staged emotion, the text withholds any moment in which she knows herself or her situation. This axis is therefore flat by design.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: The axis is well grounded in a broad critical consensus that Dulcinea del Toboso exists in the text only as an object of Quixote's discourse and Sancho's fraud — a name without a psyche. relational_axes.axis_name: From Presumed Mutual Bond to Confessed Soliloquy
relational_axes.pole_start: An ostensibly reciprocal courtship: embassies are planned, letters written, a reply awaited, a love of twelve years' standing with four modest encounters behind it.
relational_axes.pole_end: An openly unilateral devotion: the lover confesses he has never seen her or crossed her threshold and loves her 'solely by hearsay,' while weeping over an enchanted peasant he cannot restore.

trajectory.position_description: The relation is treated by Quixote as a functioning bond with a real addressee; he plans to send her a verse letter and speaks of their modest glances as a shared history.
key_moments: Chapter 22: she is the standard against which Helen is measured.
Chapter 24: a verse letter to her is promised to Sancho as messenger.
Chapter 26: the four sightings in twelve years and the admission that he imagines her as he would have her be.

trajectory.position_description: Contact is simulated entirely: a forged spoken command, then a fabricated visit, an undelivered letter and an unread one. The correspondence that appeared to constitute intimacy is shown never to have existed.
key_moments: Chapter 28: a reply and a summons are authored for her.
Chapter 31: the letter was never carried; no reply can ever have existed.
Chapter 32: the invented embassy of wheat, sweat and cheese which Quixote transfigures into pearls.

trajectory.position_description: She is honoured as a clause, a battle-cry and an oracle while Quixote's obedience migrates to Micomicona; the relation is conducted in her name by others.
key_moments: Chapter 30: she becomes a legal reservation on the Micomicona boon.
Chapter 45: her name is absent entirely; permission is sought of Dorothea.
Chapter 47: a false prophecy of marriage and sons is read as her guarantee.

trajectory.position_description: At her own doorstep the fiction of reciprocity is dismantled by Quixote himself; the bond is declared to rest on reputation alone, and Sancho withdraws his corroboration.
key_moments: Chapter 61: her real employment is overruled as an enchanter's fraud.
Chapter 62: 'I have never seen her in my life... enamoured solely by hearsay'.

trajectory.position_description: Devotion reaches maximum intensity at maximum distance: he testifies publicly that she is enchanted into a hideous peasant, vows endless tears, and finally attempts to coerce Sancho's flogging to restore her.
key_moments: Chapter 84: he confesses she is 'turned into the most ill-favoured peasant wench'.
Chapter 85: 'daughter of her own works' — he defends her being rather than her person.
Chapter 113: attempted forced flagellation to end her enchantment fails; the rescue is deferred.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the novel's cleanest trackable relational decline: every apparent channel of contact (letter, messenger, forged reply, embassy, visit) is exposed as fabricated or void, and Quixote himself names the relation hearsay at ch62. The trajectory is one-directional — intimacy thins as rhetoric inflates — which is why confidence is high.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: The shift from the fictive reciprocity of the Palomeque embassy and letters (Part I) to the openly unilateral 'de oídas' devotion and the enchanted, un-restorable peasant of Part II is one of the most thoroughly analysed relational arcs in Cervantine criticism, treated under rubrics such as idealisation, absence, self-fashioning, and the 'sweet enemy' of chivalric love. Structuralist and narratological readings of Dulcinea as a purely textual, constructed lady — the beloved who exists only in the lover's discourse and in the deeds meant to be performed for her — ground precisely the move the axis describes. The axis is therefore well supported, though scholars typically describe it as an erotics of absence rather than phrasing it as a reciprocity-to-soliloquy curve.

relational_axes.pole_start: Esteem expressed as lyric celebration: her beauty is the measure of all beauty, her name a synonym for the peerless, offered freely and with pleasure.
relational_axes.pole_end: Esteem expressed as ideology under siege: she must be vindicated by blows, by forced confessions from rivals, by 'all comparisons are odious,' and by the assertion that her virtue 'rectifies blood' — worship as enforcement.

trajectory.position_description: Her superlative status is asserted for pleasure and ornament, requiring no defence because no one contests it.
key_moments: Chapter 22: Helen would not be so famous had Dulcinea lived then.
Chapter 27: her name becomes a verse refrain on tree bark.

trajectory.position_description: Esteem becomes combative for the first time: Sancho's comparison with Dorothea earns a beating, and her worth is declared the efficient cause of Quixote's valour.
key_moments: Chapter 31: Sancho says she is 'not half as fair' as Dorothea.
Chapter 31: 'she fights in me and conquers in me' — esteem converted to doctrine.
Chapter 32: every coarse detail alchemised into proof of perfection.

trajectory.position_description: His esteem must now survive his own reports of her degradation: an enchanter is blamed for the wheat, and he publicly testifies to her hideous peasant form while maintaining her peerlessness.
key_moments: Chapter 61: the wheat-sifting attributed to an envious enchanter.
Chapter 76: 'all comparisons are odious' — Montesinos must retract a comparison.
Chapter 84: peerless lady publicly confessed to be enchanted into a wench.

trajectory.position_description: Esteem is legalistic and defensive: she is defended against doubters as 'the daughter of her own works,' her lineage argued at a ducal table, and her standing finally pursued through a coerced flogging.
key_moments: Chapter 85: 'virtues rectify blood'; vow of ceaseless tears.
Chapter 86: ducal decree reinstates her beauty and eventual proper form.
Chapter 113: an attempted forced penance undertaken on her behalf.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The level of Quixote's esteem never falls — it is the *character* of that esteem that changes, from spontaneous lyric praise to a creed requiring violence, legal argument and ducal ratification. Confidence is medium because the shift is tonal and rhetorical rather than a change in rank on the dimension.

relational_axes.axis_name: From Sole Devotional Object to Dispensable Literary Pretext
relational_axes.pole_start: Dulcinea begins as Quixote's invented, singular lady: the absent beloved whose name licenses knight-errantry and whose imagined scorn or favor organizes his quest. She is relationally central, but entirely as an object of his devotion.
relational_axes.pole_end: She ends as a dissolved pretext. Quixote's recovery of reason folds her into the 'dark shadows' of his madness; he does not renounce her with contempt, but he omits her from his confession, will, and dying words. The relation is not broken by her but dissolved with the fiction that housed it.

trajectory.position_description: She is created in Quixote's mind and invoked in borrowed literary forms. Her centrality is absolute in rhetoric but abstract in fact.
key_moments: Chapter 2: Quixote invents Dulcinea as his lady.
Chapter 3: he calls her 'Princess Dulcinea' and accuses her of scorn.
Chapter 5: her beauty becomes an article of faith to be confessed without seeing her.
Chapter 6: she is renamed into the ballad and Moorish Xarifa.

trajectory.position_description: Her name is used to bless combat, judge defeated men, and serve as a legal receipt. Quixote's relation to her is functionally central but increasingly administrative.
key_moments: Chapter 9: he commends himself to her before the windmills and Biscayan.
Chapter 10: the Biscayan is sent to her as judge.
Chapter 11: Sancho uses her name to stop Quixote's oath.
Chapter 21: Quixote commends himself to her beside God.
Chapter 23: freed convicts are ordered to El Toboso and refuse.

trajectory.position_description: Quixote admits he pictures her as he would have her be, and her name is handled through forged letters, invented replies, and legal conditions. She remains central, but the relation is openly mediated by fraud and literary convention.
key_moments: Chapter 26: Quixote says, 'I picture her in my imagination as I would have her to be.'
Chapter 31: Sancho confesses the embassy was invented.
Chapter 32: Sancho invents a Dulcinea who laughs at the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
Chapter 47: Quixote decodes a prophecy into her womb and future sons.
Chapter 49: her name becomes a conjuration he silences.

trajectory.position_description: She becomes a problem to be solved: an epitaph, a searched-for address, a counterfeit peasant, and an enchantment to be undone. Quixote's devotion remains absolute, but it is increasingly directed at a condition rather than a person.
key_moments: Chapter 53: academicians bury her in epitaph.
Chapter 61: Quixote forbids the wheat-sifting memory and relocates her to a palace.
Chapter 63: he kneels to a peasant girl as the enchanted Dulcinea.
Chapter 64: he proposes an experiment to test who can see her.
Chapter 76: in the cave she flees from him and begs by proxy.

trajectory.position_description: Her cure becomes a ducal entertainment and then a negotiated payment in Sancho's lashes. Quixote defends her name, but his devotion becomes elegiac, pastoral, and finally fraudulent in its 'completion.'
key_moments: Chapter 85: Quixote concedes 'God knows whether there be any Dulcinea or not.'
Chapter 88: she appears in Merlin's masque demanding Sancho's lashes.
Chapter 110: Altisidora curses her to remain enchanted.
Chapter 117: Quixote is defeated while defending her beauty and bound to a year of peace.
Chapter 125: Sancho's tree-whipping is counted as her cure.

trajectory.position_description: She becomes a pastoral name to be carved on trees rather than a woman to be found. When Quixote recovers reason and dies, she is absent from his will and final words; the relation ends not by rejection but by the collapse of the fiction that sustained it.
